title: Stable Prevalence of Benign HPV-Related Oral Lesions Over Four Decades: A Retrospective Clinicopathological Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives Benign human papillomavirus (HPV)-related oral lesions, including squamous papilloma, verruca vulgaris, multifocal epithelial hyperplasia, and condyloma acuminatum, are clinically and histologically overlapping entities whose long-term prevalence is poorly characterized in Middle Eastern populations. This study documented their clinicopathological profile and prevalence trends over 42 years at a regional oral pathology referral center. Methods Biopsy records (1984-2025) were retrospectively reviewed, and all benign HPV-related oral lesions were evaluated for demographic data, anatomical site, lesion type, multiplicity, and recurrence. Two oral and maxillofacial pathologists independently reviewed the slides, blinded to the original diagnoses, and assessed the findings against the WHO diagnostic criteria; HPV infection was not confirmed by molecular testing. Results Of 8790 biopsy submissions, 77 (0.88%) were benign HPV-related oral lesions. Prevalence remained stable across 6-year intervals (0.67%-1.14%), with no significant temporal trend (Cochran–Armitage test, P = .697) despite a 2-fold increase in submissions. Squamous papilloma was predominant ( n = 52, 68%), followed by verruca vulgaris ( n = 15, 19%), multifocal epithelial hyperplasia ( n = 9, 12%), and condyloma acuminatum ( n = 1, 1%). Mean age was 34.9 years (SD ± 15.4), peaking in the third decade. Male patients predominated overall (male-to-female ratio, 1.2:1), varying by lesion type. Conclusion Over four decades, benign HPV-related oral lesions maintained a stable prevalence below 1% overall, differing from rising global trends and likely reflecting population-specific sociocultural and epidemiological factors. The study also summarizes distinguishing features and existing prevalence data. These findings from an underrepresented region support future molecular epidemiological studies to establish population-specific prevalence benchmarks.

title: Pre-implementation assessment of upstream domains on the uptake of HPV self-sampling in safety-net settings: a scoping review.
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) screening can be used as an early detector for cervical cancer. The newly US Food and Drug Administration-approved HPV self-sampling tests can be used by safety net practices in the USA to help mitigate the current screening disparities seen in patients. As patient acceptability and capability have already been established, this scoping review synthesizes the barriers and facilitators of implementing HPV self-sampling from the perspective of safety net providers and leadership, and the upstream factors not yet explored in current research. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a literature search was conducted exploring peer-reviewed publications and grey literature to establish the current landscape of HPV self-sampling. Findings were organized using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. From the 57 works included, it was found that safety net practices are capable of implementing HPV self-sampling by utilizing current workflows and team members. However, outer setting guidelines and policies heavily influence the implementation process, likely causing a delay in uptake by safety net practices. Recent guideline endorsements and forthcoming insurance coverage address several of these barriers, making post-approval implementation research in safety net settings an urgent priority.

title: Health Economic Impact and Cost Threshold for Switching From Bivalent to Nonavalent HPV Vaccination for Preadolescent Girls in KwaZulu Natal, South Africa: A Mathematical Modeling Analysis Accounting for the HIV Epidemic.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Human papillomavirus bivalent (2vHPV) and nonavalent (9vHPV) vaccines protect against HPV types causing 70% and 90% of cervical cancers, respectively. South African guidelines recommend vaccinating girls ages 9-14 with 1 dose of 2vHPV. Switching recommendations to 9vHPV could avert more cervical cancer burden, but the cost-effectiveness and cost-threshold of 9vHPV in South Africa is unknown. METHODS: Using a validated compartmental HPV and HIV transmission model parameterized to KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, we simulated scenarios of 2vHPV and 9vHPV implementation over 100 years with 2 doses (72% coverage) and 1 dose (80% and 90% coverage) with lifelong or waning single-dose vaccine efficacy. We evaluated cervical cancer cases and deaths averted. We also estimated the maximum cost/dose for 9vHPV to be cost-effective using willingness-to-pay thresholds from $500/disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted to $3015/DALY averted (2023 USD). We also assessed the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios of 9vHPV at current costs ($110/dose) compared with 2vHPV ($9.23/dose). RESULTS: Single-dose 9vHPV at 80% coverage could avert 7.9% more cervical cancer cases and 6.4% more deaths than 2vHPV (lifelong efficacy). The maximum 9vHPV price to be cost-effective (lifelong efficacy, 80% coverage) ranged from $15 ($500/DALY averted threshold) to $45/dose ($3015/DALY averted threshold). At current market costs, single-dose 9vHPV at 90% coverage exceeds commonly used cost-effective thresholds with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios of $10,480/DALY averted (lifelong efficacy) and $8806/DALY averted (waning efficacy). CONCLUSIONS: Implementing 9vHPV can result in a greater reduction in cervical cancer burden than 2vHPV, but vaccine costs need to be reduced for 9vHPV to be cost-effective in KwaZulu-Natal.
journal: Journal of acquired immune deficiency syndromes (1999)

title: Premature Mortality Across Cervical and Noncervical HPV-Associated Cancers in SEER Registries.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Premature mortality comparisons across human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated cancers may inform prevention, but converting case-based HPV fractions to years of potential life lost (YPLL) requires assumptions about HPV-specific outcomes. METHODS: We analyzed 179,568 SEER 17 tumor records diagnosed in 2000-2018 using recorded cancer-specific deaths within five years. Site-specific case fractions defined a reference YPLL75 allocation. We examined case-composition standardization, attribution fractions, HPV-status outcome differences, cutoffs of 70, 75, and 80 years, sex and race/ethnicity subgroups, and descriptive equity decomposition, using 5,000 patient-cluster bootstrap replicates. RESULTS: The unstandardized non-cervical/cervical index increased from 0.818 to 0.935. Case-age-standardized indices decreased from 0.932 to 0.830 (change, -0.102; 95% bootstrap interval, -0.165 to -0.043). Reference final-period indices were 0.781 for YPLL70 and 1.069 for YPLL80. A hypothetical decline in the oropharyngeal HPV-related/unrelated mean-YPLL ratio from 1.00 to 0.50 yielded an unstandardized change of -0.004 (-0.063 to 0.053). Reference standardized Black-White, low-high county-income, and nonmetro-large metro gaps were 185.3, 103.4, and 38.9 YPLL75 per 100 calculable records; their directions persisted across examined allocation scenarios. CONCLUSIONS: Within these SEER records, non-cervical cancers contributed substantial premature mortality. Cervical/non-cervical balance and period comparisons depended on case composition, attribution, HPV-status outcome assumptions, and the YPLL cutoff. Equity contrasts were more consistent in direction; decomposition did not identify causal pathways.

title: Combination of BVAC-C and durvalumab in recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer: a phase II study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors show limited efficacy in previously treated recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer (rmCC). BVAC-C is an autologous B cell-based and monocyte-based therapeutic vaccine targeting human papillomavirus (HPV)16/18 E6 and E7 oncoproteins. METHODS: We report a phase II trial—representing the first clinical evaluation of a B cell– and monocyte-based therapeutic HPV vaccine combined with a programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor—evaluating BVAC-C combined with durvalumab in patients with HPV16/18-positive rmCC who had progressed after platinum-based chemotherapy. This single-arm, open-label, two-part phase II trial was registered prospectively at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04800978) on 15 March 2021, before enrollment of the first participant. RESULTS: 30 patients received treatment; 29 were evaluable for efficacy. The objective response rate (ORR) was 37.9% (six complete responses and five partial responses), and the disease control rate was 62.1%. The 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 51.7% and median PFS was 8.7 months (95% CI 4.0 to 24.3 months). Patients with a treatment-free interval >6 months achieved a significantly higher ORR (52.9% vs 16.7%; p=0.047). Notably, the median duration of response was 20 months and complete responders showed sustained remission beyond 18 months, raising the possibility of functional cure in a subset of patients. Antigen-specific T-cell responses and cytokine activation were robust and PD-L1-independent. CONCLUSIONS: BVAC-C plus durvalumab showed encouraging antitumor activity with a manageable safety profile, supporting further evaluation in HPV-positive rmCC. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT04800978.

title: Performance of a DNA methylation marker panel in cervical samples from women with abnormal cytology findings
abstract: Background Reliable triage methods are essential in cervical cancer screening to avoid overtreatment. DNA methylation markers offer an objective molecular readout with potential to keep false-positive rates low. We evaluated the GynTect ® DNA methylation assay as a triage marker in cervical samples from women with abnormal cytology, in comparison with the p16/Ki-67 Dual Stain test CINtec Plus ® . Methods Surplus liquid-based cytology samples from 1,000 women with cytology ≥ PAP III (Low-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion = LSIL, or worse) were tested with GynTect ® (markers: ASTN1, DLX1, ITGA4, RXFP3, SOX17, ZNF671). cobas ® HPV and p16/Ki-67 Dual Stain (CINtec Plus ® ) results were available for all samples; histopathology was available for a subset of 601 samples. Positivity rates with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the Wilson score method. Results Overall GynTect positivity was 27.7% versus 88.3% for p16/Ki-67 Dual Stain. Methylation positivity correlated with cytological severity: 17.0% in LSIL, 30.2% in moderate High-​Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion HSIL, and 65.0% in the PAP IV group (high-grade SIL/AIS and HSIL suspicious for invasion). Among HPV16/18-positive samples, 38.4% were GynTect-positive versus 94.8% p16/Ki-67 Dual Stain-positive. By histopathology, GynTect positivity was 15.0% (CIN I), 27.0% (CIN II), and 56.5% (CIN III); all four cancer cases were GynTect- and p16/Ki-67 Dual Stain​-positive. Of 191 GynTect-positive cases with histopathology, 73% had CIN II or CIN III. Conclusions GynTect positivity (27.7%) was significantly lower than p16/Ki-67 Dual Stain positivity (88.3%), with a statistically significant monotonic trend across increasing cytological severity (Cochran-Armitage trend test, p < 0.001) and histopathological categories (p < 0.001). All four histologically confirmed carcinomas were GynTect-positive. These findings are consistent with a potential role for GynTect in selective triage after abnormal cytology, with lower positivity rates suggesting higher selectivity for high-grade disease compared with p16/Ki-67 Dual Stain. Prospective validation in primary HPV-screening triage populations is required to determine whether this translates into clinical benefit.

title: HPV-associated macrophage states and expression-based scores in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) status defines contrasting immune ecosystems in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). We investigated how tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) states and their regulatory programs contribute to this diversity and whether these features can be captured in patient-level expression signatures. We integrated 229,196 single cells from 59 patients with HNSCC (26 HPV-positive and 33 HPV-negative), defined eight TAM states, and combined functional and trajectory analyses with regulon inference, virtual perturbation, and CellChat. A 12-gene Weighted Inflammatory Score (WIS) and a TAM-related score (TRS) were evaluated in independent transcriptomic cohorts. Multiplex immunofluorescence provided representative tissue-level observations. HPV-positive tumors showed a lymphoid-enriched landscape, whereas HPV-negative tumors had greater TAM and fibroblast representation. Patient-level comparisons identified lower Inflammatory TAM and Pro-tumor/Secretory TAM fractions in HPV-positive patients (Benjamini–Hochberg [BH]-adjusted p = 0.0172 and 0.0486, respectively). Regulon analysis and virtual SNAI1 perturbation converged on inflammatory, leukocyte migration, and chemotaxis programs. Targeted CellChat analysis identified a candidate epithelial-source HLA-DRA–CD4 interaction involving seven TAM recipient states in HPV-positive tumors compared with two in HPV-negative tumors. Fixed-coefficient WIS achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.938 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.863–1.000) across 36 independent patients. TRS provided complementary HPV-status discrimination, with a cross-validated AUC of 0.783 in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and an external AUC of 0.649 in GSE40774. HPV-associated immune differences in HNSCC involve distinct macrophage states, candidate SNAI1-linked inflammatory and migratory regulatory programs, and inferred epithelial–TAM communication patterns. WIS and TRS connect selected single-cell observations with patient-level transcriptomic features and may guide future mechanistic and validation studies.

title: A multipathogen view of Epstein-Barr virus pathogenesis and tumorigenesis.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 95% of the global population and contributes to multiple human cancers and autoimmune diseases. Co-infection with pathogens including Helicobacter pylori, human immunodeficiency virus, human papillomavirus, and Plasmodium falciparum can reshape host immunity and the EBV latency-lytic balance and, in some settings, promote reactivation. Collectively, these interactions may exacerbate chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, and epigenetic dysregulation to accelerate disease progression and tumor formation. Existing clinical treatments control only the active pathogens but fail to target latent EBV. Emerging strategies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) gene editing and EBV-targeted immunotherapy aim to eliminate latent viral reservoirs. This review outlines the synergistic mechanisms of EBV co-infection in oncogenesis, highlighting that further research on pathogen interactions is vital for developing better prevention and treatment options.

title: Population-level indirect effects of HPV vaccination in high-income settings: a Bayesian modelling study
abstract: Summary Background Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination provides direct protection to vaccinated individuals, but also indirectly protects unvaccinated individuals through reduced HPV transmission. Mechanistic transmission models that predict the magnitude of such effects have been crucial to informing vaccination strategies. However, nearly two decades of post-vaccination experience in high-income countries now allow us to empirically characterise how population-level indirect effects vary with vaccine coverage, time since vaccine introduction, and age. Methods We synthesised studies reporting HPV16/18 prevalence before and after vaccine introduction in high-income settings between 2007 and 2025. Indirect effects were estimated as the observed reduction in HPV16/18 prevalence after accounting for expected direct vaccine protection. We used a Bayesian hierarchical model to examine associations with vaccine coverage, time since vaccine introduction, and age at effect assessment across routine, catch-up, and non-targeted vaccination groups. XGBoost was used as a complementary, non-parametric approach. Findings Data from 11 high-income settings were included. Indirect effects increased during the first five to eight years after vaccine introduction and then remained relatively stable. Indirect effects generally decreased with increasing vaccine coverage. Patterns with age differed across vaccination groups. In the routine group, indirect effects increased during adolescence and remained positive at older observed ages. In the catch-up group, indirect effects decreased with age and approached zero or became negative after approximately age 25 years. XGBoost identified similar non-linear patterns. Interpretation Indirect protection against HPV16/18 develops gradually after vaccine introduction and varies with vaccine coverage, age, and vaccination group. This empirical approach can complement transmission models by using real-world evidence to characterise population-level indirect protection. However, making predictions outside the populations and ranges represented in the data should be done cautiously. Funding This study received no specific funding. Research in context Evidence before this study We searched PubMed for studies published up to Oct 26, 2026. The search terms were (“HPV vaccin” [All Fields] OR “human papillomavirus vaccin” [All Fields]) AND (“herd immunity” [All Fields] OR “herd effect” [All Fields] OR “indirect effect” [All Fields] OR “indirect protection” [All Fields] OR “herd protection” [All Fields]). We included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies, and modelling studies that assessed the indirect effects of HPV vaccination on HPV infection or HPV-related outcomes. We excluded studies that focused exclusively on direct vaccine protection or economic evaluations that included herd immunity without separately estimating or reporting indirect effects. We identified 301 articles, of which 77 met the inclusion criteria: 52 observational studies, 22 modelling studies, and three systematic reviews or meta-analyses. From those studies, two systematic reviews by Drolet and colleagues (2015 and 2019) synthesised evidence from 14 high-income countries and provided evidence of herd protection following vaccine introduction. A meta-analysis of results from 16 transmission dynamic models by Brisson and colleagues (2016) projected substantial herd effects under different vaccination coverage levels. More recently, an observational study by Meglic and colleagues (2026) used nationwide registry data from Sweden and found age-varying herd effects, with lower incidence of high-grade cervical lesions among unvaccinated women in cohorts exposed to school-based vaccination. Despite growing real-world evidence from high-income countries over nearly two decades, few studies have examined how indirect protection varies with vaccination coverage, time since programme introduction, and age across settings. Added value of this study To our knowledge, this is the first study to synthesise real-world HPV16/18 prevalence data from 11 high-income settings to estimate the indirect effects of HPV vaccination over the period 2007–2025. Our findings show that indirect protection generally increases during the first several years after vaccine introduction before stabilising, with different patterns across age groups and vaccination programmes. Implications of all the available evidence As countries work towards cervical cancer elimination, understanding the indirect protection provided by HPV vaccination is important for assessing its broader population-level impact. This multi-country evidence complements transmission-dynamic models and provides an empirical basis for evaluating the long-term effects of HPV vaccination programmes.

title: Harnessing OmpF and GroEL as leader proteins to engineer bacterial membrane vesicles for antigen delivery and anti-tumor immunity induction.
abstract: Tumor vaccines are designed to activate tumor antigen-specific cellular immunity, thereby restoring the body's intrinsic capacity for immune surveillance and clearance of tumor cells. However, the efficacy of vaccines has been largely limited in clinical settings due to the complex immunosuppressive mechanisms orchestrated by tumors, which impede the induction of potent anti-tumor effector responses. Recently, bacterial membrane vesicles (BMVs) have gained attention as promising vaccine vectors owing to their nanoscale vesicle structure, which facilitates antigen delivery, and the presence of inherent pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that provide potent immune stimulation. Nevertheless, low efficiency of antigen loading remains a major obstacle to the broad application of BMVs in vaccine development. This study aimed to identify a new leader protein for engineering BMV-based tumor vaccines. Bacterial proteins GroEL and OmpF were fused to the tumor antigen HPV 16 E7 and expressed in E. BMVs were subsequently prepared using high-pressure homogenization. The physicochemical and immunogenic properties of these engineered BMVs, along with their potentials for tumor immunotherapy, were evaluated both in vitro and in vivo. Results indicated that GroEL and OmpF effectively directed the modification of HPV 16 E7 on BMVs. The engineered BMVs promoted dendritic cell maturation, induced tumor-specific immune responses, and significantly suppressed the growth of grafted TC-1 tumors in mice. In conclusion, GroEL and OmpF represent highly promising leader proteins for developing efficient BMV-based antigen delivery systems for cancer vaccination.

title: Changing patterns of gynaecological cancer incidence and mortality in Sri Lanka, 2005–2022: a national population-based registry study
abstract: Background Gynaecological cancers are an important public health concern, yet evidence on their epidemiological patterns and temporal trends in Sri Lanka remains limited. This study evaluated trends in incidence and mortality and characterised histological patterns across gynaecological cancer sites. Methods This population-based study used Sri Lanka cancer registry data and national mortality data for 2005–2022. Age-standardised incidence (ASIR) and mortality (ASMR) rates were calculated using the World Health Organization world standard population. Joinpoint regression was used to estimate annual and average annual percent changes (APC/AAPC) with 95% confidence intervals. Histological distribution was assessed for the major cancer sites. Results A total of 48,603 gynaecological cancer cases were recorded, led by cervical (n = 18,013), ovarian (n = 15,765), and uterine (n = 12,766) cancers. Overall ASIR increased from 18.62 to 29.95 per 100,000, with an AAPC of 3.25% (95% CI: 2.30–4.41; p < 0.001). Uterine cancer showed the steepest increase (AAPC 8.21%; 95% CI: 7.01, 10.04; p < 0.001), followed by ovarian cancer, whereas cervical cancer incidence remained stable (p = 0.53). Vulval, vaginal, and other unspecified female genital cancers also showed significant increases in age-standardised incidence. Uterine cancer accounted for the highest number of deaths (n = 4,115) with a non-significant decline (AAPC − 0.80%). Cumulative risk increased most markedly for corpus uteri cancer, with significant trends in both age groups, and for vaginal cancer among women aged 0–74 years. Histology was predominantly squamous cell carcinoma for cervical cancer (77.8%), while adenomas and adenocarcinomas predominated in uterine corpus cancer (73.1%). Cystic, mucinous, and serous neoplasms were the most common ovarian histological group (44.1%). Conclusion Sri Lanka's gynaecological cancer burden is shifting, with a growing contribution from uterine and ovarian cancers alongside a persistent cervical cancer burden, in the context of demographic and metabolic transitions. These findings support strengthening organised cervical cancer screening and sustained human papillomavirus vaccination while expanding diagnostic and treatment capacity for uterine and ovarian cancers.

title: The Experience of Social Stigma in Women with HPV: A Qualitative Systematic Review and Meta-ethnography
abstract: Abstract Background & Objective: High-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is the primary etiological driver of cervical neoplasia. However, its sexually transmitted nature enmeshes the clinical trajectory with profound social stigma, shame, and moral surveillance. This meta-ethnography systematically synthesized global qualitative evidence on women’s lived experiences of HPV-related stigma across diverse sociocultural contexts. Methods Following Noblit and Hare’s seven-phase meta-ethnographic framework and adhering to PRISMA and eMERGe/ENTREQ guidelines, systematic searches were executed across international (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Embase, ProQuest) and Persian databases up to 2026. After screening and JBI critical appraisal, 21 primary qualitative studies were synthesized via reciprocal translation, refutational exploration, and lines-of-argument synthesis. Results Analysis of first- and second-order constructs yielded nine descriptive themes and four overarching third-order analytical themes: (1) Gendered and Moralized Corporeal Stigma (pathology conflated with sexual promiscuity, asymmetric blame, and spoiled feminine identity); (2) Clinical and Institutional Stigma (secondary symbolic trauma, provider moral judgment, and commercial objectification); (3) Relational Stigma and the Disclosure Paradox (the dilemma between seeking spousal support and risking abandonment or marital rupture); and (4) Dynamic Trajectory and Transformative Agency (a dialectical shift from acute corporeal shame to cognitive decoupling, spiritual reframing, health literacy acquisition, and post-traumatic growth). Conclusion HPV-related stigma is a multi-layered, structural phenomenon that operates as a mechanism of gendered social control, substantially undermining screening and therapeutic adherence. title: HPV vaccination hesitancy among adolescent girls and caregivers in Rwanda
abstract: Abstract Background Vaccination against human papillomavirus (HPV) is a highly effective way to prevent cervical cancer. Rwanda has achieved high HPV vaccination coverage through a school-based program, but vaccine hesitancy may threaten sustained uptake. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of HPV vaccine hesitancy among adolescent girls aged 13–15 years and their caregivers, and to identify factors associated with hesitancy, to inform service delivery. Methods We conducted a nationally representative cross-sectional household survey in all 30 districts of Rwanda between July and October 2025. Adolescent girls aged 13–15 years and their caregivers were selected through multistage cluster sampling and interviewed separately using standardized questionnaires. Informed by the WHO SAGE framework, respondents were classified as hesitant if the girl was unvaccinated or if they reported unwillingness or uncertainty about vaccination, unwillingness to recommend the vaccine, or perceiving it as less than very important; caregivers were also asked about vaccine safety and family and friends’ support. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression identified associated factors. Results A total of 2,651 adolescent girls and 2,744 caregivers were included (household response rate 94.1%; 89% among girls and 94% among caregivers); 2,241 caregivers had complete hesitancy data. HPV vaccine hesitancy was 15.9% (95% CI: 14.0–17.9) among adolescent girls and 29.1% (95% CI: 26.7–31.7) among caregivers. Among girls, being aged 14 years (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.66, 95% CI 0.50–0.87) or 15 years (aOR 0.58, 0.40–0.82) rather than 13 years, attending school (aOR 0.16, 0.11–0.23), and living in the Northern (aOR 0.57, 0.34–0.97) or Southern Province (aOR 0.52, 0.34–0.80) were associated with lower odds of hesitancy, whereas Protestant affiliation was associated with higher odds (aOR 1.64, 1.24–2.19). Among caregivers, rural residence (aOR 0.63, 0.45–0.89), a male household head (aOR 0.61, 0.39–0.95) and a previously married household head (aOR 0.60, 0.41–0.87) were associated with lower odds of hesitancy. Conclusions HPV vaccine hesitancy persists in Rwanda among both girls and caregivers despite high coverage. Outreach to out-of-school girls, engagement of faith leaders, and caregiver-focused communication, particularly in higher-hesitancy provinces and urban areas, could help sustain progress towards cervical cancer elimination.

title: Integrative approach in management of rare Buschke-Lowenstein tumor (Giant Condyloma): A case report.
abstract: Buschke-Lowenstein Tumor (BLT) is an uncommon, slow-growing verrucous lesion associated with Human Papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11, often mimicking malignancy due to its locally aggressive nature and high recurrence rate. The uniqueness, is the successful integration of Ayurveda and modern medical therapies in the management of a recurrent BLT, demonstrating a holistic and recurrence-free outcome. A 77-year-old male presented with multiple exophytic, foul-smelling growths involving the groin and scrotal region, accompanied by persistent pain, itching, and seropurulent discharge for three months. Previous dermatological treatments provided no relief. Clinical and histopathological findings confirmed Giant Condyloma (Buschke-Lowenstein Tumor). Ayurvedic assessment correlated the condition with Vrushana Kacchu progressing to Charmakeela, characterized by Vata-Kapha dominance. The treatment protocol was integrated with Ayurvedic internal medications (Cap. Grab, Aragwadadi Kashaya), external therapies (Pentabark Kashaya) and shastra karma (Chedana Karma followed with Agnikarma) along with modern antibiotic coverage. The patient achieved complete healing with minimal scarring and showed no recurrence during a two-year follow-up period. This case highlights the effectiveness of an integrative approach that combines Ayurvedic surgical techniques with a conventional postoperative antibiotic regimen in the management of BLT. The recurrence-free outcome demonstrates that integrative medicine can serve as a practical and effective model for treating chronic and recurrent tumors, promoting optimal healing and improving patient satisfaction.
journal: Journal of Ayurveda and integrative medicine

title: HPV prevalence and risk factors in a population-based cervical cancer screening program in Tashkent, Uzbekistan.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Population-based evidence on high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) and cervical screening outcomes in Uzbekistan is limited. We assessed hrHPV prevalence, district variation, associated factors, and cytological findings in Tashkent. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 52,995 women aged 18-70 years attending routine cervical screening across Tashkent city during 2024-2025. HR-HPV testing was performed using real-time PCR; reflex liquid-based cytology was performed for all HPV-positive women. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent determinants of HPV positivity (n = 52,995) and cytological abnormality (n = 2,255 HPV-positive women with adequate cytology). RESULTS: Overall HR-HPV positivity was 4.43% (95% CI: 4.26-4.61%), with significant heterogeneity across districts (p < 0.01); Bektemir district recorded the highest prevalence. Independent predictors of HPV positivity included older age (aOR 2.41, 95% CI 1.24-4.83, for 56-70 years), irregular menstruation (aOR 1.39, 95% CI 1.23-1.57), and early sexual debut, while barrier contraception (aOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.81) and grand multiparity (aOR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65-0.98) were protective. Among HPV-positive women, any cytological abnormality was detected in 24.6% and high-grade lesions in 17.3%. Keratosis was the strongest predictor of cytological abnormality (aOR 4.09-5.16, both p < 0.01). CONCLUSIONS: This large population-based study establishes a comprehensive HPV epidemiological baseline for Tashkent and demonstrates the clinical yield of HPV-primary screening with reflexive cytology triage. District-level heterogeneity and identified risk profiles provide evidence for geographically targeted program optimization in support of Uzbekistan's progress toward WHO 90-70-90 cervical cancer elimination targets.

METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 52,995 women aged 18-70 years attending routine cervical screening across Tashkent city during 2024-2025. HR-HPV testing was performed using real-time PCR; reflex liquid-based cytology was performed for all HPV-positive women. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent determinants of HPV positivity (n = 52,995) and cytological abnormality (n = 2,255 HPV-positive women with adequate cytology). RESULTS: Overall HR-HPV positivity was 4.43% (95% CI: 4.26-4.61%), with significant heterogeneity across districts (p < 0.01); Bektemir district recorded the highest prevalence. Independent predictors of HPV positivity included older age (aOR 2.41, 95% CI 1.24-4.83, for 56-70 years), irregular menstruation (aOR 1.39, 95% CI 1.23-1.57), and early sexual debut, while barrier contraception (aOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.81) and grand multiparity (aOR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65-0.98) were protective. Among HPV-positive women, any cytological abnormality was detected in 24.6% and high-grade lesions in 17.3%. Keratosis was the strongest predictor of cytological abnormality (aOR 4.09-5.16, both p < 0.01). CONCLUSIONS: This large population-based study establishes a comprehensive HPV epidemiological baseline for Tashkent and demonstrates the clinical yield of HPV-primary screening with reflexive cytology triage. District-level heterogeneity and identified risk profiles provide evidence for geographically targeted program optimization in support of Uzbekistan's progress toward WHO 90-70-90 cervical cancer elimination targets.

title: Sexual Violence/Abuse and Cervical Cancer: A Systematic Review of the Relationship.
abstract: Sexual violence/abuse may influence cervical carcinogenesis through increased human papillomavirus exposure, trauma-related immune dysregulation and reduced engagement with prevention and care. However, the evidence on the co-occurrence of cervical cancer and sexual violence/abuse has not been systematically synthesised. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus, PsycArticles, EMBASE and Scopus were searched for English-language studies published between January 2000 and January 2025. Studies were eligible if they reported the prevalence of cervical cancer among survivors of sexual violence/abuse or vice versa. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Seven studies from community, primary care and gynaecological oncology settings met inclusion criteria, covering a population of 8,840 participants. Among survivors of sexual violence/abuse, cervical cancer prevalence ranged from 5.4% to 32.3% and was consistently 1.5 to 2.7 times higher than among non-exposed comparators within the same settings. Among cervical cancer populations, sexual violence/abuse prevalence ranged from 18.4% to 57.5%, with stronger associations observed for severe or penetrative exposures. Adjusted odds ratios and relative risks ranged from approximately 3.3 to 11.15 at the highest exposure levels, consistent with a dose-response pattern. Findings point to a need for prevention strategies that consider how gender intersects with exposure to sexual violence/abuse. The review also suggests elevated co-occurrence between cervical cancer and sexual violence/abuse relative to global population estimates (~10% intimate-partner violence and ~6% non-partner violence). Limitations include small samples and measurement heterogeneity. Findings support co-produced, survivor-centred and trauma-informed approaches to cervical cancer prevention and oncology care that address barriers to healthcare engagement. Larger studies using validated measures and confounder-aware designs are needed.

title: Data from The mRNA-Based Therapeutic Vaccine NTX250 Induces Potent Antitumor Immunity in HPV-Driven Cancers
abstract: UNLABELLED: Human papillomavirus (HPV) plays a pivotal role in various malignancies, including cervical, anogenital, head, and neck cancers. Despite the availability of highly effective prophylactic vaccines, many individuals remain susceptible to HPV-driven cancers because of barriers such as limited vaccine access, lack of awareness, or personal preferences. Current treatments primarily target lesions without eradicating persistent HPV infections, leading to an increased risk of subsequent HPV-associated cancers. This scenario underscores an urgent need for innovative treatment modalities aimed at eliminating persistent HPV infections. In this study, we developed NTX250, a messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutic platform engineered to deliver HPV type 16 (HPV16) E6 and E7 antigens, in conjunction with the immunomodulators interleukin (IL) 12 and LIGHT. A lipid and ionizable peptoid nanoparticle system facilitated precise intralesional delivery of NTX250. Localized NTX250 administration in HPV16-transformed tumor-bearing models led to complete tumor regression and established durable, antigen-specific immune memory. Replacing the HPV antigens with a construct comprising colorectal cancer cell-specific neoepitopes enabled stimulated antitumor immunity and suppressed tumor growth, supporting the generalizability of the approach. Overall, NTX250 represents a promising nonsurgical immunotherapy platform that is capable of eliciting robust and targeted antitumor immune responses across diverse malignancies. This adaptable mRNA nanoparticle approach enables the codelivery of tumor-specific antigens and immunomodulators, with the potential to target tumor-associated antigens beyond HPV. SIGNIFICANCE: NTX250 is an mRNA-based therapeutic platform that offers a noninvasive approach to eradicate persistent HPV infections and induce strong antitumor immune responses, fulfilling a critical need in HPV-related cancer treatment.

title: Beyond the Cervix: HPV Vaccine Attitude Profiles and Cancer Prevention Knowledge Gaps Among Vietnamese Medical Students.
abstract: Medical students will be central to communicating human papillomavirus (HPV)-related cancer prevention as Viet Nam introduces HPV vaccination into its national immunization program. This study identified HPV vaccine attitude profiles among Vietnamese medical students, compared their knowledge of HPV-related cancers across profiles, and explored a brief tool to support tailored education. In a cross-sectional survey of 727 medical students conducted in May-June 2026, latent class analysis of 10 attitude items identified four profiles: Comprehensive Trust (25.7%), Selective Trust (29.0%), Passive Acceptance (42.4%), and Hesitant & Skeptical (2.9%). Hesitant & Skeptical students had the lowest HPV and HPV vaccine knowledge, whereas Selective Trust and Passive Acceptance did not differ in any knowledge domain. Across all profiles, knowledge was concentrated on cervical cancer: 79.1% of students recognized HPV as a cause of cervical cancer, compared with 44.0% for penile, 29.6% for anal, and 19.1% for oral cancer, and 25.0% did not recognize that males can be infected. A four-item classification tree reproduced profile membership with 88.9% accuracy (Cohen's κ = 0.83) in a held-out test set, although its sensitivity for the Hesitant & Skeptical profile was 50.0%. Medical students shared a cervix-centered understanding of HPV-related cancer but differed in their attitudes toward vaccination. Medical curricula should teach HPV-related cancers in both sexes to all students and add profile-informed counseling training; the four-item tool may help educators tailor this training but requires external validation.

title: Association between seminal HPV DNA detection and bacterial profiles in infertile men.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Human papillomavirus (HPV) detection and seminal microbial dysbiosis are associated with impaired semen quality, through mechanisms involving oxidative stress and inflammation. METHODS: Semen samples from infertile men were analyzed for HPV DNA using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Predominant bacterial genus was identified through 16S rRNA gene PCR amplification and sequencing. Pro-inflammatory cytokine and oxidative stress markers were quantified. The dielectric properties of DNA were evaluated by electrical bioimpedance spectroscopy (EBiS). RESULTS: Seminal HPV DNA was detected in 73% of semen samples. The Shannon-Wiener diversity index revealed significantly greater bacterial diversity in HPV DNA positive samples compared with HPV DNA negative samples (2.54 vs. The most frequently identified bacterial genera were Enterococcus (34.5%), Pseudomonas (12.1%), and Escherichia (10.3%). The HPV DNA negative group exhibited a significantly higher relative abundance of Enterococcus than the HPV DNA positive group (62.5% vs. These microbial shifts were accompanied by increased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, evidence of oxidative DNA damage, and poorer semen quality parameters. CONCLUSIONS: Seminal HPV DNA associated changes in relative abundance of seminal bacteria may contribute to male infertility.

title: HPV Vaccination by Health Insurance and Usual Source of Care Status among US Young Adults
abstract: Health insurance and a usual source of care may identify different groups of young adults with low human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination coverage. Their joint associations with vaccination were examined using the 2022 National Health Interview Survey. The complete-case sample comprised 2,131 adults aged 18–26 years. Participants were classified by insurance coverage and the presence of a usual place for healthcare. Survey-weighted logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race and ethnicity, and education; predictive margins summarized adjusted vaccination prevalence and absolute differences. Adjusted prevalence was 51.0% among insured participants with a usual source of care, 43.2% among insured participants without one, 37.3% among uninsured participants with a usual source, and 23.8% among uninsured participants without one. Compared with participants having both forms of access, those having neither had a 27.2-percentage-point lower adjusted prevalence (95% CI, −37.9 to −16.5). The corresponding difference among insured participants without a usual source was −7.8 points (95% CI, −14.6 to −0.9), although this group's odds-ratio association weakened after adjustment for recent physician contact. There was no clear evidence of multiplicative interaction (P=0.380). Joint classification identified a substantial vaccination gap among young adults lacking both insurance and a usual source of care. Current access measures and lifetime vaccination histories do not establish temporal or causal relationships.

title: Conditional survival of patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma according to p16 status.
abstract: Studies have shown that Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is associated with better Overall Survival (OS) in Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OPSCC). We assessed Conditional Survival (CS) to verify whether the prognostic advantage of p16-positive (HPV+) remains over time. A retrospective cohort study conducted at two Brazilian oncologic centers. Variables included were sex, age, ethnicity, smoking/alcohol consumption, p16-status, clinical-stage. Survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier considering all-cause (OS) and Cancer-Specific (CSS) survival. CS was defined as the probability of surviving an additional two years given survival up to time t, calculated as CS(2|t) = S(t + 2)/S(t). Log-rank was applied to compare curves. RESULTS: Of 1295 patients with OPSCC, 62.4% were p16-negative (HPV-) (n = 808); 37.6% HPV+ (n = 487). 5-year OS for HPV+ was 74.6%, and 36.2% for the HPV- [p < 0.001]. Differences in CS between HPV+/HPV- decreased over time, becoming non-significant at CS(2|4) [p = 0.083], primarily observed in CSS. Differences disappeared earlier among men at CS(2|3) [p = 0.116]. Older patients showed greater improvement in CS. Differences in CS among HPV+/HPV- stage IV disappeared at CS(2|3) [p = 0.388] but re-emerged at CS(2|4), when HPV- surpassed HPV+ (CS(2|4): 93.3% vs. Differences between HPV+/HPV- diminished earlier among smokers at CS(2|2) [p = 0.446], while among drinkers this occurred later, CS(2|4) [p = 0.600]. CONCLUSIONS: CS improved over time among HPV- OPSCC, particularly among those who survived the first three years after diagnosis, reducing the prognostic difference in survival compared with HPV+. Further studies assessing CSS and long-term CS beyond five years in HPV+/HPV- patients are warranted to better clarify the role of HPV and established risk factors.

title: Integrating Binary Silva Classification and Tumor Size for Predicting Survival in Early-Stage HPV-Associated Endocervical Adenocarcinoma
abstract: Background The optimal risk stratification for early-stage human papillomavirus-associated endocervical adenocarcinoma (HPVA) lacking conventional major high-risk factors remains clinically challenging. This study aimed to evaluate the independent prognostic utility of the binary Silva classification in this specific population and to develop a validated progression-free survival (PFS) nomogram for individualized risk assessment. Methods We retrospectively evaluated 163 patients with FIGO 2018 stage IA2–IIA2 HPVA who underwent radical surgery and lacked major high-risk pathological factors (e.g., lymph node metastasis). Patients were categorized into low- and high-risk binary Silva groups based on morphological invasive patterns and lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) status. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression was utilized to identify independent prognosticators. A predictive PFS nomogram was constructed and internally validated utilizing 1,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples to calculate optimism-corrected performance metrics. Results Over a median follow-up of 48 months (95% CI, 40–59), the high-risk binary Silva group (n = 82) exhibited significantly inferior PFS and overall survival compared with the low-risk group (n = 81; P < 0.001 and P = 0.0015, respectively). Multivariable analysis confirmed that high-risk binary Silva status (hazard ratio [HR], 4.37; 95% CI, 1.64–11.62; P = 0.003) and tumor size ≥ 2 cm (HR, 4.05; 95% CI, 1.57–10.42; P = 0.004) were robust independent adverse predictors for PFS. The resulting two-factor predictive nomogram demonstrated favorable internal validity, yielding an optimism-corrected concordance index (C-index) of 0.717. Conclusion The binary Silva classification serves as a powerful, independent prognostic stratifier for early-stage HPVA without major high-risk factors. By integrating binary Silva status with tumor size, our internally validated nomogram provides a quantitative, practical framework to refine postoperative risk assessment and potentially guide individualized adjuvant treatment strategies.

title: Diagnostic Target Selection in Selected Sexually Transmitted and Associated Urogenital Infections: Implications for TaqMan PCR
abstract: Diagnostic target selection must account for sequence variation, target loss, taxonomic coverage, and viral genome structure. This selective narrative review compares evidence from Chlamydiatrachomatis, Gardnerella spp., Ureaplasma urealyticum, and HPV16 to identify implications for TaqMan PCR design, validation, and reporting. Documented chlamydial escape variants demonstrate that complementary targets must address a specified failure mechanism and preserve detection under the assay’s reporting rule. Gardnerella studies show that the reported taxon must match the species groups actually detected, while Ureaplasma assays require both within-species inclusivity and discrimination from U. HPV comparisons do not establish universal superiority of E6/E7 over L1 and show why assay discordance alone cannot demonstrate regional target loss. The review links these findings to case-specific validation material and illustrates their application in a dual-target chlamydial design. The resulting recommendations distinguish correction of an inaccurate reporting label, additional testing of incompletely represented populations, and modification of an assay with confirmed detection failure. Evidence from different assay chemistries and clinical endpoints is interpreted separately; the proposed validation approach has not been prospectively evaluated.

title: Hepatitis B Vaccine as a Primary Prevention Strategy for Cancer: Mechanisms, Outcomes and Model Extension
abstract: Vaccination against Hepatitis B can prevent liver cancer by preventing chronic infection of the liver. This paper reviews the role of hepatitis B virus (HBV) in hepatocellular carcinoma, cancer prevention via vaccination, and lessons learned from China's experience for other cancer-prevention programmes. HBV promotes cancer by inducing chronic inflammation in the host, integrating viral DNA into the host's DNA, and altering cell regulation through viral proteins. China's childhood vaccination programme has reduced infections among young children significantly. Extended data from the Qidong trial have also indicated a decrease in primary liver cancer; however, due to a small number of cancer cases, the exact extent remains unknown. Comparison with human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination shows that the biological principle can be applied to infections, but delivery needs to match the age and circumstances of the target population. China's addition of HPV vaccination to the national programme in 2025 is a policy change. Disease spread can be effectively prevented through timely vaccination, accessible medical services, and ongoing care for high-risk groups.

title: The TGF-β/ID1 Signaling Pathway Axis Mediates HPV E6/E7 Induced Malignant Transformation of Mammary Epithelial Cells
abstract: Abstract Breast cancer is the most prevalent malignancy among women worldwide. Increasing evidence implicates human papillomavirus (HPV) in breast cancer, particularly HPV16 and HPV18. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the role of the TGF-β/ID1 signaling axis in HPV16/18 E6/E7 mediated malignant transformation of mammary epithelial cells. Stable MCF-10A cell lines expressing E6/E7 were established. E6/E7 expression promoted malignant transformation of mammary epithelial cells. RNA sequencing revealed extensive transcriptional reprogramming, with enrichment of cell cycle and DNA replication pathways. Gene set enrichment analysis and flow cytometry confirmed accelerated cell cycle progression, with increased S and G2/M phase populations. Mechanistically, E6/E7 upregulated TGFB2 and enhanced SMAD3 phosphorylation, indicating activation of canonical TGF-β signaling. TGFB2 silencing reduced SMAD3 activation and suppressed proliferation. E6/E7 also induced the downstream target ID1, whereas TGFB2 knockdown decreased ID1 expression. ID1 depletion inhibited proliferation and induced cell cycle arrest. In summary, E6/E7 promotes cell cycle progression and tumor initiating capacity via activation of the TGFB2–TGF-β–ID1 axis, providing mechanistic insight into HPV associated breast malignant transformation.

title: Data from Integrated Organoid CRISPR Screening Reveals NF1 as a Gatekeeper of Cervical Squamous Malignant Transformation
abstract: UNLABELLED: Cervical cancer can progress from high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions driven by persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Identifying the gatekeepers restraining malignant transformation could reveal strategies to prevent and treat cervical cancer. In this study, we integrated single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-Cas9 screening, and organoid modeling to dissect this process. Single-cell analysis of patient samples revealed progressive activation of rat sarcoma virus (RAS) and proliferation programs along epithelial differentiation paths. A focused CRISPR screen in HPV-positive pretumoroids identified neurofibromin 1 (NF1) as the top suppressor of malignant transition. NF1 loss accelerated carcinogenesis in organoids, substantially shortening the experimental interval required for the emergence of malignant phenotypes and recapitulating basal cell expansion, altered differentiation marker expression, and tumorigenicity. Mechanistically, NF1 loss enhanced RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase and phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B signaling, promoted proliferative programs, and remodeled chromatin accessibility at regulatory regions enriched for activator protein 1 motifs. Conversely, NF1 restoration in cancer organoids induced apoptosis and suppressed malignant maintenance. Artificial intelligence-guided modeling was used to design a minimal NF1-derived peptide predicted to interact with RAS GTP-binding protein. The NF1-GAP-mimetic peptide reduced tumor organoid viability and cervical lesion-associated bioluminescence in an HPV16-driven mouse model and was associated with local immune-related changes without marked alterations in selected splenic T-cell populations. Together, these findings establish NF1 as a critical constraint on HPV-associated epithelial evolution and provide a time-compressed organoid model of cervical carcinogenesis, offering proof of concept for NF1-inspired therapeutic interception of RAS-associated signaling. SIGNIFICANCE: Single-cell atlas and organoid screening identified NF1 loss as a driver of cervical carcinogenesis, which can be rescued with an AI-designed NF1 mimetic peptide that offers a therapeutic paradigm to intercept tumorigenesis.

title: Plasma Protein Signature in Cervicovaginal Fluid Reflects the Severity of HPV-Associated Cervical Transformation
abstract: Cervical cancer progresses from persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection through low-grade (LSIL) and high-grade (HSIL) squamous intraepithelial lesions to invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), yet current triage tools—cytology, HPV genotyping, and colposcopy—cannot reliably distinguish lesions that need surgical intervention from those that regress. Cervicovaginal fluid (CVF) directly contacts the cervical transformation zone and is an attractive, non-invasively collected substrate for biomarker discovery. Comprehensive label-free proteomic profiling (HPLC-DDA-PASEF-MS/MS) of CVF was performed in 93 women spanning the full histological spectrum of HPV-associated cervical disease: HPV-negative controls (NILM, n = 18), HPV-positive inflammatory disease of the cervix (IDC, n = 17), LSIL (n = 20), HSIL (n = 20), and SCC (n = 18). Of 1,476 proteins detected (1,219 quantified), 106 CVF proteins met strict criteria (≥3 unique peptides) and differed significantly in at least one pairwise comparison (IDC, LSIL, HSIL, SCC vs. The CVF proteome underwent progressive remodeling with disease severity, with the number of differentially expressed proteins (DEPs, |FC| > 2, p < 0.05) rising from 13 in IDC and 6 in LSIL to 43 in HSIL and 100 in SCC relative to NILM. The most robust discrimination between disease requiring intervention (HSIL and SCC) and conditions suited to surveillance (NILM, IDC, and LSIL) was driven not by epithelial proteins but by a coordinated plasma protein signature—CPN2, ORM2, AGT, KNG1, F2, ITIH1, GC, APOA1, SERPINA1, and C4A—all among the top 5% most abundant plasma proteins, reflecting epithelial barrier disruption, acute-phase response, and hemostatic activation. Pathway analysis converged on platelet activation and degranulation, complement and coagulation cascades, neutrophil degranulation, IGF transport and uptake, and keratinization across comparisons. TRIM29 (R = −0.63) and AHNAK2 (R = −0.61) showed the strongest negative correlations with lesion grade, whereas IGHM (R = 0.55), AGT (R = 0.53), and ITIH1 (R = 0.53) increased with grade. A subset of proteins, including ACTN4, PSMA3, ACP1, EIF5AL1, IGFBP2, KNG1, EIF5A, and ORM2, overlapped between inflammatory and neoplastic processes, indicating that HPV-driven inflammation alone can partially mimic a neoplastic CVF signature. These data position CVF proteomics as a promising non-invasive approach for triaging HPV-associated cervical pathology and suggest that a multi-protein panel centered on the APOA1/ORM2/KNG1/SERPINA1 axis, combined with grade-associated epithelial proteins such as TRIM29 and AHNAK2, warrants validation in independent, well-characterized cohorts.

title: Prediction of Occult Invasive Cervical Cancer After Conization for High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesions: Model Development, Temporal Validation, and a Web-Based Tool
abstract: Abstract Objective This study aimed to develop and temporally validate a prediction model for occult invasive carcinoma in patients with cervical high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) undergoing conization and to develop a web-based prediction tool for individualized risk assessment. Methods We retrospectively included patients with cervical HSIL who underwent conization and were subsequently classified as having invasive carcinoma or non-upgraded disease according to the final histopathological findings. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression were used for candidate predictor selection. Multivariable logistic regression and several machine-learning algorithms were developed and evaluated using internal cross-validation, followed by temporal validation in an independent cohort.The selected model was subsequently implemented as an R Shiny–based web prediction tool. Results Invasive carcinoma was detected after conization in approximately 6% of patients with cervical HSIL. LASSO selection identified age, high-grade cytology on TCT, HPV-16/18 positivity, involvement of 3–4 cervical quadrants, CIN2 or CIN3 on endocervical curettage (ECC), and CIN3 on biopsy as candidate predictors. In multivariable logistic regression, high-grade cytology, HPV-16/18 positivity, involvement of 3–4 quadrants, and CIN2 or CIN3 on ECC remained independently associated with histopathological upgrade. Among the evaluated algorithms, AdaBoost achieved the highest AUC in internal cross-validation and it was implemented as a web-based tool that provides individualized predicted probabilities and threshold-based risk classification using six routinely available preoperative variables. Conclusion Approximately 6% of patients with cervical HSIL in this cohort had occult invasive carcinoma identified after conization. Prediction models incorporating clinical and pathological variables showed good discriminative performance in the derivation cohort and retained satisfactory performance in temporal validation. A web-based prediction tool was subsequently developed to facilitate individualized risk assessment and may support clinical risk stratification for patients with cervical HSIL before conization.

title: Comparative performance of three HPV DNA detection assays for cervical cancer screening in Algeria.
abstract: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is the principal etiological driver of cervical cancer, making accurate HPV detection central to contemporary screening strategies. This study compared three molecular assays-INNO-LiPA HPV Genotyping Extra, Cobas 4800 HPV, and Amplicor HPV-using overlapping cervical-sample subsets from Algerian women at increased risk of cervical disease. Among the 94 specimens tested by both INNO-LiPA and Cobas, HR-HPV was detected in 54.3% and 29.8%, respectively; INNO-LiPA also identified HPV16 and HPV18 more frequently. In the 18-specimen subset tested by all three assays, HR-HPV positivity was 27.8% with INNO-LiPA, 33.3% with Cobas, and 50.0% with Amplicor. Pairwise agreement ranged from weak to substantial (κ=0.116-0.667), and discordance was significantly associated with multiple HPV infections (OR=5.88, 95% CI 1.29-26.85; p=0.012). HR-HPV positivity was more frequent in specimens with abnormal cytology, with the strongest association observed for INNO-LiPA (OR=4.9, 95% CI 1.5-15.9; p=0.005). Using the study-defined composite reference classification, INNO-LiPA showed higher sensitivity (93%) but lower specificity (62%) than Cobas (71% and 88%, respectively). These findings demonstrate substantial assay-dependent variation in HR-HPV detection and highlight the value of detailed genotyping for epidemiological investigation, while supporting the use of clinically validated HR-HPV assays for screening applications.

title: The Contribution of a Health Society to Immunization in Saudi Arabia: a Community Case study of the Waey Association for Community Health
abstract: Background: Non-Profit Organizations (NPOs) are long-standing partners in immunization, yet documented examples from state-led health systems remain scarce. This case study examines how a Saudi health society contributes to immunization through a surge workforce and vaccine demand beyond childhood. Methods: A community case study was conducted through document analysis of the program documentation of the Waey Association for Community Health, compiled for the 8th Saudi International Vaccination Forum (Riyadh, 2026). Activity domains were profiled against an explicit inclusion rule, reported outputs were converted into derived indicators, and each domain was coded against seven NPO roles drawn from a global scoping review; the findings were then synthesized into an explanatory model. Results: Six immunization domains addressing coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), human papillomavirus (HPV), seasonal influenza, and adult vaccination were identified, alongside two supporting activities. Deployment to COVID-19 vaccination centers mobilized 313 volunteers for 24,778 hours (79.2 hours per volunteer); the 2024 to 2025 community vaccination program mobilized 336 volunteers for 9,628 hours and reached 14,281 beneficiaries through 17 activities. The COVID-19 deployment thus supplied 72.0% of combined hours from 48.2% of volunteers. Four of seven NPO roles were represented, led by service delivery and demand generation. Conclusions: The society functioned as a reservoir of trained surge capacity and as a channel for vaccine demand among adolescents and adults. Both functions drew on shared assets, and a minimum reporting standard covering doses, unique beneficiaries, volunteer hours, and population denominators would allow them to be evaluated.

title: The role of biomarkers in predicting treatment outcomes after therapy for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and early-stage cervical cancer: a scoping review
abstract: Background High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion/cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (HSIL/CIN2–3) and early-stage cervical cancer require different treatments and have distinct recurrence and surveillance profiles. Biomarker research predicting treatment outcomes is fragmented across biomarker classes, specimen types, populations, and outcome definitions, with prognostic and predictive roles often conflated. This scoping review aimed to map research on biomarkers predicting treatment outcomes after therapy for HSIL/CIN2–3 and early-stage cervical cancer from 2000 to 2026, and to classify biomarkers as diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, or monitoring. Specifically, the review addressed three research questions: (1) which biomarkers have been evaluated against treatment outcomes for HSIL/CIN2–3 and for early-stage cervical cancer, and how do the two evidence bases compare; (2) how are these biomarkers distributed across diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, and monitoring roles; and (3) which biomarker categories are sufficiently mature and homogeneous to be considered candidates for future meta-analysis. Methods The review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework, refined by Levac et al., and JBI methodology, and was reported according to PRISMA-ScR. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched for studies published from January 2000 to January 2026. Eligible studies evaluated viral, molecular, immunohistochemical, serum, radiologic, or immune biomarkers against treatment outcomes in women with HSIL/CIN2–3 or FIGO stage I–IIB2 cervical cancer. Two reviewers independently screened and charted data by population, biomarker class, specimen type, evidentiary role, and outcome. Findings were synthesized narratively and in tables without meta-analysis. Results Among 58 representative sources, HSIL studies mainly evaluated persistent/type-specific high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) DNA, HPV E6/E7 mRNA, HPV integration, p16/Ki-67 dual staining, and host-gene methylation, predominantly as diagnostic, monitoring, or prognostic markers. In invasive cancer, the investigated biomarkers included serum SCC-Ag, circulating tumour HPV DNA, tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, sentinel lymph node micrometastases, microRNAs, and PD-L1 combined positive score. Conclusion Biomarker research remains heterogeneous and is dominated by prognostic and monitoring applications, with limited evidence for genuinely predictive biomarkers. Standardized terminology, harmonized reporting, population-specific analyses, and treatment-comparison designs are needed to advance biomarker-guided individualized management.

This scoping review aimed to map research on biomarkers predicting treatment outcomes after therapy for HSIL/CIN2–3 and early-stage cervical cancer from 2000 to 2026, and to classify biomarkers as diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, or monitoring. Specifically, the review addressed three research questions: (1) which biomarkers have been evaluated against treatment outcomes for HSIL/CIN2–3 and for early-stage cervical cancer, and how do the two evidence bases compare; (2) how are these biomarkers distributed across diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, and monitoring roles; and (3) which biomarker categories are sufficiently mature and homogeneous to be considered candidates for future meta-analysis. Methods The review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework, refined by Levac et al., and JBI methodology, and was reported according to PRISMA-ScR. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched for studies published from January 2000 to January 2026. Eligible studies evaluated viral, molecular, immunohistochemical, serum, radiologic, or immune biomarkers against treatment outcomes in women with HSIL/CIN2–3 or FIGO stage I–IIB2 cervical cancer. Two reviewers independently screened and charted data by population, biomarker class, specimen type, evidentiary role, and outcome. Findings were synthesized narratively and in tables without meta-analysis. Results Among 58 representative sources, HSIL studies mainly evaluated persistent/type-specific high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) DNA, HPV E6/E7 mRNA, HPV integration, p16/Ki-67 dual staining, and host-gene methylation, predominantly as diagnostic, monitoring, or prognostic markers. Conclusion Biomarker research remains heterogeneous and is dominated by prognostic and monitoring applications, with limited evidence for genuinely predictive biomarkers. Standardized terminology, harmonized reporting, population-specific analyses, and treatment-comparison designs are needed to advance biomarker-guided individualized management.

title: Integrated Bulk and Single Cell Transcriptomics Reveal That CD48 Marks an Immune Activated Microenvironment and Predicts Favorable Prognosis in Cervical Cancer
abstract: Abstract Cervical cancer is driven by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus ( HPV ), and treatment options for recurrent or metastatic disease remain limited because immune checkpoint inhibitors benefit only a subset of patients. Reliable prognostic markers are therefore still needed. Here we integrated TCGA-CESC bulk transcriptomes with the GSE168652 single-cell dataset to screen immune-related cervical cancer targets (IRCTs) through weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), machine-learning feature selection, and survival modeling, and then characterized the expression, prognostic value, and immune-microenvironment associations of the core gene. CD48 was selected as the consensus core gene by multiple algorithms, and its high expression was associated with longer overall survival (multivariate Cox HR = 0.498, 95% CI 0.302–0.822, p = 0.006). High CD48 coincided with elevated immune scores, increased infiltration of immune effector cells, and upregulation of several immune checkpoint molecules. Single-cell analysis showed that CD48 was expressed mainly in CD8 + T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and monocytes/macrophages, whereas epithelial or tumor cells were nearly negative. Virtual knockout further showed that loss of CD48 significantly perturbed the cytotoxic effectors NKG7 and GZMA. These findings identify CD48 as a candidate marker that reflects an immune-activated microenvironment and carries independent prognostic value in cervical cancer.

title: Probiotics for Vaginal Dysbiosis and Recurrent Bacterial Vaginosis: A Narrative Review of Strain-Specific Evidence
abstract: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a common manifestation of vaginal dysbiosis, and recurrence after antimicrobial therapy remains frequent. This narrative review examines the rationale for restoring vaginal lactobacilli and evaluates oral and intravaginal interventions using selected clinical trials, evidence syntheses, and practice guidance. In a phase 2b trial, intravaginal Lactobacillus crispatus CTV-05 following metronidazole reduced 12-week recurrence from 45% to 30%. Trials of oral Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GR-1 plus Limosilactobacillus reuteri RC-14 reported inconsistent short-term cure outcomes. Meta-analyses suggest a reduction in BV recurrence with some preparations, with uncertainty arising from differences in strains, formulations, timing, and outcome definitions. Small trials of vaginal prebiotic gels report improvements in microbiological measures, while evidence for durable benefit remains limited. Available data provide insufficient support for extrapolating BV findings to vulvovaginal candidiasis, human papillomavirus clearance, or shiitake-derived adjuncts. The clearest evidence concerns specific interventions tested after standard BV treatment. Future trials should measure symptomatic recurrence alongside strain persistence and assess whether protection persists after dosing ends.

title: Understanding Cervical Screening Engagement Among Young South Asian Women: Perspectives of Women and Healthcare Professionals.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite increased uptake of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, cervical screening participation among younger South Asian women has declined, particularly in deprived areas in England. The reasons for this pattern remain poorly understood. This study explored barriers and facilitators to cervical screening among South Asian women aged 25-29 in a deprived locality. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with South Asian women aged 25-29 (n = 15) and healthcare professionals involved in cervical screening delivery (n = 6) in Blackburn with Darwen. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. RESULTS: Barriers to screening were multifactorial and included limited understanding of cervical screening and HPV, cultural norms surrounding modesty and sexuality, fear of community judgement and embarrassment, and structural challenges such as appointment access and competing responsibilities. Family networks acted as both barriers and facilitators. Healthcare professionals described adapting language to reduce fear, but highlighted service pressures related to staffing and funding, which constrained proactive engagement. Although most women reported receiving the HPV vaccination, understanding of HPV and the continued importance of cervical screening remained limited, highlighting opportunities to reinforce cervical screening education. CONCLUSION: Cervical screening engagement among young South Asian women is shaped by intersecting cultural, emotional, and structural influences, which may be intensified in deprived settings. HPV vaccination should be accompanied by clear communication about the continued importance of cervical screening, particularly where knowledge and awareness remain low. Culturally responsive communication, flexible service provision and community partnership approaches are needed to address persistent inequalities in screening uptake. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: The study was informed by prior community engagement and public involvement work with underserved populations. Interview guides were developed in collaboration with a public advisor from the South Asian community to ensure they were relevant, inclusive, and reflective of community priorities.

title: Dental public health in action: A regional response to oral cancer in the South West of England.
abstract: Head and neck cancer is an increasing public health concern in England, with incidence and mortality rates rising and variation by geography, age, sex and deprivation. Oral cancer forms part of this disease burden and shares modifiable risk factors including tobacco use, alcohol consumption and, for some tumour sites, human papillomavirus infection. The South West reflects these national concerns, with some areas experiencing oral cancer incidence rates above the national average. This paper presents an overview of a regional dental public health response to support prevention, earlier detection and system wide action on oral cancer in the South West of England. The work included development of intelligence tools such as oral cancer profiles, snapshot infographics, an evidence-informed regional oral cancer framework with accompanying action plan, a prevention focused webinar for dental and oral health improvement teams, and targeted oral cancer training for HPV vaccination teams. The intelligence tools, framework and action plan provided a structure for healthcare systems to assess oral cancer trends and inequalities, incorporate oral cancer within needs assessments and strategies, strengthen collaborative working with stakeholders, and improve professional awareness of oral cancer risk factors and referral routes for suspected lesions. Early process-based outcomes suggest engagement across dental, oral health improvement and vaccination workforces, with feedback indicating that participants valued content on patient communication, risk-factor reduction and signposting. Future work should focus on embedding oral cancer within local needs assessments, sustaining prevention activity addressing risk factors, and upskilling wider workforces to strengthen early detection.

title: Vaccination Attitudes Among Adolescents in Lithuania: The Role of Previous Vaccination Experiences, Awareness and Beliefs, and Information Sources
abstract: Background/Objectives: Vaccination attitudes developed during adolescence may influence later health-related decisions. This study examined vaccination attitudes and associated factors among Lithuanian adolescents. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 340 adolescents aged 10–19 years from eight schools assessed vaccination experiences, parental involvement, information-related factors, and six attitude items. An exploratory three-item Positive Vaccination Attitude Score (PVAS; range 0–100) was used to summarise perceived safety, benefit–harm balance, and effectiveness. Associations were examined using cumulative link models and multivariable ordinary least squares regression with heteroscedasticity-consistent type 3 (HC3) robust standard errors, multiple-comparison adjustment and sensitivity analyses. Results: Reported vaccination uptake was 88.8% for routine childhood vaccines, 47.1% for additional non-mandatory vaccines, and 38.5% for COVID-19 vaccines. Only 43.2% of participants considered vaccination information sufficient, 25.6% reported independently seeking vaccination-related information, and 18.2% reported having heard of human papillomavirus (HPV). Neutral responses predominated regarding vaccine safety (60.6%), benefit–harm balance (70.0%), and effectiveness (70.0%). The exploratory PVAS demonstrated high internal consistency (ordinal α = 0.910; ω = 0.917), although further validation is needed. Adolescents who had not received COVID-19 vaccination or were unsure of their vaccination status had lower adjusted PVAS scores than vaccinated adolescents (β = −13.10, 95% confidence interval (CI) −19.47 to −6.72; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Older age was associated with lower PVAS scores before multiple-comparison adjustment (β = −5.10; p = 0.041), but this association was no longer statistically significant after Holm correction (p = 0.408). The statistical significance of the association with COVID-19 vaccination status was sensitive to certain assumptions regarding clustering within schools. Conclusions: Vaccination attitudes among the participating adolescents were heterogeneous. The association between COVID-19 vaccination status and PVAS scores warrants cautious interpretation given the cross-sectional design and uncertainty related to clustering within schools. The PVAS remains an exploratory measure requiring independent psychometric validation.

title: HPV-Associated Epigenetic Reprogramming in Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Molecular Mechanisms, Circulating Biomarkers and Clinical Translation
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) has become the dominant form of oropharyngeal cancer in many high-income countries and is now recognised as a biologically and clinically distinct entity with markedly better survival than its tobacco-related counterpart. Beyond the canonical inactivation of p53 and pRb by the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7, HPV profoundly remodels the host and viral epigenomes. HPV-positive tumours display a hypermethylated landscape, including a CpG island methylator-like phenotype that targets Polycomb repressive complex 2 genes, alongside altered histone-modifying activity, chromatin remodelling and deregulated non-coding RNA networks. Methylation of the viral genome itself, particularly of the upstream regulatory region and E2 binding sites, tracks with integration and oncogene expression. These changes shape the tumour immune microenvironment and treatment response. They also leave traces in the circulation: circulating tumour HPV DNA, methylated cell-free DNA and extracellular-vesicle microRNAs are emerging as tools for diagnosis, risk stratification and post-treatment surveillance. This review summarises current knowledge of HPV-driven epi-genetic reprogramming in OPSCC, evaluates the analytical and clinical validity of epigenetic and viral liquid-biopsy biomarkers, and discusses their translation into treatment de-escalation, epigenetic therapy, immunotherapy com-binations and nutri-epigenetic modulation.
