title: Differential serum proteome profiling and electrochemical biosensing of leucine-rich alpha-2-glycoprotein (LRG1) and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) as subtype-specific biomarkers for HPV-negative cervical cancer
abstract: Background Cervical cancer (CC) is still a major global health concern. Specifically, human papillomavirus (HPV) - negative CC (HPV-neg CC) has a poorer prognosis than HPV-positive cases (HPV-pos CC). Distinguishing between HPV-pos and HPV-neg CC is the focus of this study, using proteomics and electrochemical biosensors. Methods Pooled serum samples from healthy individuals, HPV-pos CC, and HPV-neg CC patients were analyzed using label-free quantitative proteomics. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were analyzed using PEAKS ® Studio software (≤1% False Discovery Rate, FDR; 1.5-fold change threshold). STRING and Metascape databases were used for protein-protein interaction analysis and functional clustering. An electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) biosensor was developed to quantify potential candidate biomarkers including lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) and leucine-rich alpha-2-glycoprotein (LRG1). Results Proteomics revealed distinct signatures, associating HPV-pos and HPV-neg CC with humoral immune response impairment and systemic inflammatory response, respectively. Concurrently, inflammatory mediators, LBP and LRG1 were top DEPs across all groups, with 3.99 and 2.89-fold increases in HPV-neg CC vs. healthy control, respectively. The EIS-based biosensor verified that LBP had remarkable discriminatory power in separating HPV-pos CC cases from HPV-neg CC cases (AUC = 0.9815), whereas LRG1 successfully separated cancer cases from healthy controls (AUC = 1.000). Conclusions Proteomics and EIS biosensor techniques identified LBP as a potential biomarker linked to systemic inflammatory responses in HPV-neg CC. Therefore, this pilot study links the gap between proteomic discovery and clinical application, eventually providing exploratory insights into subtype characterization for HPV-neg CC. Further investigations in a larger cohort based on our findings are necessary for a better understanding of the role of LBP and LRG1 in all CC subtypes.

source_records.abstract: Background Cervical cancer (CC) is still a major global health concern. Specifically, human papillomavirus (HPV) - negative CC (HPV-neg CC) has a poorer prognosis than HPV-positive cases (HPV-pos CC). Distinguishing between HPV-pos and HPV-neg CC is the focus of this study, using proteomics and electrochemical biosensors. Methods Pooled serum samples from healthy individuals, HPV-pos CC, and HPV-neg CC patients were analyzed using label-free quantitative proteomics. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were analyzed using PEAKS ® Studio software (≤1% False Discovery Rate, FDR; 1.5-fold change threshold). STRING and Metascape databases were used for protein-protein interaction analysis and functional clustering. An electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) biosensor was developed to quantify potential candidate biomarkers including lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) and leucine-rich alpha-2-glycoprotein (LRG1). Results Proteomics revealed distinct signatures, associating HPV-pos and HPV-neg CC with humoral immune response impairment and systemic inflammatory response, respectively. Concurrently, inflammatory mediators, LBP and LRG1 were top DEPs across all groups, with 3.99 and 2.89-fold increases in HPV-neg CC vs. healthy control, respectively. The EIS-based biosensor verified that LBP had remarkable discriminatory power in separating HPV-pos CC cases from HPV-neg CC cases (AUC = 0.9815), whereas LRG1 successfully separated cancer cases from healthy controls (AUC = 1.000). Conclusions Proteomics and EIS biosensor techniques identified LBP as a potential biomarker linked to systemic inflammatory responses in HPV-neg CC. Therefore, this pilot study links the gap between proteomic discovery and clinical application, eventually providing exploratory insights into subtype characterization for HPV-neg CC. Further investigations in a larger cohort based on our findings are necessary for a better understanding of the role of LBP and LRG1 in all CC subtypes.

title: Chemosensitization Effect of Ribociclib, a CDK4/6 Inhibitor, on In Vitro Cervical Cancer
abstract: Objective Dysregulation of cell-cycle control mechanisms plays an important role in the development of many cancers, including cervical cancer. After the role of CDK 4/6 in cell cycle control and carcinogenesis was elucidated, CDK 4/6 inhibitors were developed. Ribociclib is a selective CDK4/6 inhibitor, and although its activity has been investigated in several malignancies, its potential role in cervical cancer remains incompletely defined. This study aimed to evaluate the chemosensitizing effects of ribociclib when combined with cisplatin and paclitaxel in a single human papillomavirus type 18 (HPV18)-positive cervical cancer cell line. Material and Methods For the experimental model, only the HPV18-positive human cervical adenocarcinoma-derived HeLa cell line (ATCC CCL-2) was used. Cells were treated for 24 hours with ribociclib (25 μM), cisplatin (100 μM) plus paclitaxel (2 μM), or cisplatin (100 μM) plus paclitaxel (2 μM) plus ribociclib (25 μM). Untreated cells served as controls. Cell viability was assessed using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay. Markers of angiogenesis, proliferation, apoptosis, and metastatic behavior were evaluated by immunocytochemical staining for VEGF, CDK4, CDK6, Ki-67, Bax, Bcl-2, caspase-3, E-cadherin, vimentin, fibronectin, and MMP-9. Results After 24 hours, cell viability was 48% in the cisplatin plus paclitaxel group and 55% in the cisplatin plus paclitaxel plus ribociclib group. Thus, the addition of ribociclib did not further reduce cell viability compared with chemotherapy alone. Addition of ribociclib to chemotherapy significantly reduced Bcl-2, vimentin, and MMP-9 expression and increased caspase-3 expression compared with chemotherapy alone. No significant additional reductions in VEGF or Ki-67, nor significant additional increases in Bax or E-cadherin, were observed with ribociclib. Conclusion In this single-cell-line, 24-hour in vitro model, ribociclib combined with cisplatin and paclitaxel was associated with changes in selected markers of apoptosis and metastatic behavior, despite not producing lower MTT-measured cell viability than chemotherapy alone. These findings constitute hypothesis-generating preclinical evidence and require validation in additional HPV18-positive and other cervical cancer models, in animal studies, and, ultimately, in clinical studies before any translational conclusions can be drawn.

title: Demographic Profile, Risk Factors and Histopathological Characteristics of Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia
abstract: Background: Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN) is a spectrum of ocular surface epithelial lesions ranging from dysplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors include Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and other forms of immunosuppression, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, chronic ocular surface inflammation, smoking and exposure to certain occupational or environmental irritants. Early treatment and histopathological assessment of the excised specimen is important to reduce morbidity. Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted in the Department of Oculoplasty and Ocular Oncology, Ispahani Islamia Eye Institute and Hospital from 1st September 2021 to 28th February 2022. A total of 32 patients with OSSN were included using purposive convenient sampling. Patients were clinically evaluated and underwent surgical excision, followed by histopathological examination. Postoperative follow-up was performed at the 1st, 14th postoperative days, 4th, 6th weeks and at 6 months. Results: Among 32 patients, 13 (40.6%) were above 60 years, 7 (21.9%) were aged 51–60 years, 8 (25%) were aged 41–50 years, and 4 (12.5%) were aged 31–40 years. Males predominated, with 21 (65.6%) cases compared with 11 (34.4%) females. Sunlight exposure was reported in 43.75%, smoking in 37.5%, exposure to chemical agents 3.13% and 15.63% were suffered from malnutrition. Leukoplakic type of OSSN was most predominant 22 (68.75%) and 26 (81.25%) patients presenting with cornea, limbus, and conjunctival surface involvement. Histopathology showed mild dysplasia in 12 (37.5%), moderate dysplasia in 10 (31.3%), severe dysplasia in 4 (12.5%) and invasive squamous cell carcinoma in 6 (18.8%). Conclusion: OSSN predominantly affected older males, with sunlight exposure and smoking being the common reported risk factors. Histopathology demonstrated a spectrum from mild dysplasia to invasive carcinoma.

source_records.title: Demographic Profile, Risk Factors and Histopathological Characteristics of Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia
source_records.abstract: Background: Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN) is a spectrum of ocular surface epithelial lesions ranging from dysplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors include Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and other forms of immunosuppression, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, chronic ocular surface inflammation, smoking and exposure to certain occupational or environmental irritants. Early treatment and histopathological assessment of the excised specimen is important to reduce morbidity. Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted in the Department of Oculoplasty and Ocular Oncology, Ispahani Islamia Eye Institute and Hospital from 1st September 2021 to 28th February 2022. title: Individualized Homoeopathic Treatment of Cutaneous Warts: A Case Report
abstract: Warts are the growth of skin resulting from human papillomavirus infection. These may be single, multiple, smooth, or cauliflower?like and are generally treated by applying medicine externally or surgical excision procedure. Homoeopathy has a major role in the treatment of warts and most of the homoeopathic doctor?s treat warts without external application. Case summary: We present here a case report of a 70-year-old male with warts on the neck for 6 years. The present case was completely cured within 3months of regular treatment with individualized homoeopathic medicine without any adverse effects. After detailed case taking, Causticum 200C was administered. The Modified Naranjo criteria for Homoeopathy (MONARCH) was used for assessing causal attribution, where the score was +8, suggesting that the clinical improvement was the result of the homoeopathic treatment. Before and after treatment photographs were taken to assess the improvement. This evidence-based case could pave way for further research into using individualised homoeopathy for Warts.
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

title: Google inject and the correction paradox: Fact-check uptake increased, but so did vaccine hesitancy
abstract: Vaccine hesitancy remains a pressing public health challenge, intensified by the widespread circulation of online misinformation. Although fact-checking has proven effective in correcting false claims, users rarely interact with fact-checks. This paper examines the effectiveness of Google Inject , a browser plugin that injects contextual fact-checks from 70 International Fact-Checking Network-accredited organizations directly into search results, in addressing Human Papillomavirus vaccine hesitancy. In an online simulated search environment study, 128 participants were randomly assigned to either an experimental condition in which contextual Google Inject fact-checks were injected into search results, or a control condition without them. Participants completed two simulated search scenarios targeting distinct antecedents of vaccine hesitancy — confidence and complacency . Fact-checks by Google Inject were approximately nine times more likely to be selected than standard search results; however, this selection did not translate into longer reading time or extensive scrolling behavior. Unexpectedly, Google Inject selection was associated with increased vaccine hesitancy accompanied by heightened constraints, whereas standard credible results selection was associated with a reduction in hesitancy and complacency. These findings highlight that particular design characteristics of fact-check interventions can play a critical role in shaping user responses and may inadvertently undermine corrective efforts if not carefully aligned with user motivations and informational needs.

title: Nomograma de tiempo libre de lesión en mujeres positivas al virus del papiloma humano
abstract: Introduction: Human papillomavirus infection is the main causal factor in the genesis of cervical lesions. Objective: To design and validate a nomogram to predict lesion-free survival in human papillomavirus-positive women. Material and Methods: Prospective cohort study (January 2020–December 2024) of 78 human papillomavirus-positive women without initial lesion; 6-months follow-up; event; and histological diagnosis of cervical lesion. Kaplan–Meier was estimated, curves were compared with log-rank, and a multivariate Cox model was fitted. The model was internally validated by bootstrap (1,000 replicates) and K-fold cross-validation (K=5). A nomogram was constructed from the final model and its discriminatory capacity was evaluated using time-dependent ROC curves at 24 and 40 months. Results: Of 78 women, 16 (20.5%) developed a lesion during follow-up. The independent variables in the final model were: postcoital bleeding (HR=14.99; 95%CI: 3.24–69.39), Chlamydia trachomatis infection (HR=10.13; 95%CI: 2.53–40.63), and genotype 16 (HR=3.65; 95%CI: 1.21–10.97). Model C-index (concordance): 0.849. The nomogram showed a time-dependent AUC = 0.82 (95%CI: 0.65–0.97) at 24 months and AUC = 0.87 (95%CI: 0.77–1.00) at 40 months (best performance at 40 months). Bootstrap internal validation corrected optimism, maintaining an adjusted C-index of ≈0.837. Conclusions: The nomogram facilitates estimating individual risk of developing cervical lesions among HPV-positive women and shows better discriminatory capacity at 40 months than at 24 months, reinforcing its usefulness for long-term surveillance.

title: Cervical Cytology and HPV Genotypic Risk Among Indigenous Women in San Martín, Peru: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Indigenous women in the Peruvian Amazon are underrepresented in cervical cancer research. We characterized cervical cytology and human papillomavirus (HPV) genotypes in 90 clinical records from a source population described as Awajún, Kichwa, and Shawi women; individual community affiliation was unavailable. This cross-sectional secondary analysis linked cytology and Allplex HPV28 results within participant records. No normal cytology reports were represented. Cytology-report groups comprised unspecified squamous atypia or low-grade-compatible findings (68.9%), high-grade-compatible or glandular abnormalities (5.6%), and unspecified cytology (25.6%). HPV was detected in 39 women (43.3%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 33.6–53.6%). Among HPV-positive women, 41.0% had coinfections; 92.3% (95% CI: 79.7–97.3%) carried study-defined high/probably high-risk genotypes, whereas 76.9% carried an International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) Group 1 genotype. HPV-68 was the most frequently detected genotype, occurring in seven HPV-positive women (17.9%; 95% CI: 9.0–32.7%). In exploratory analyses, no statistically significant association was detected between cytology-report grouping and study-defined high/probably high-risk HPV detection (p = 0.156; Cramér’s V = 0.209) or IARC Group 1 detection (p = 0.191). Individual molecular internal-control and histological follow-up data were unavailable. These findings cannot establish population prevalence, screening performance, or prevention gaps. Larger studies with standardized cytology and follow-up are needed.
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

title: From Bench to Bedside: Clinical Translation of Electrochemical Biosensors for Viral Diagnostics
abstract: Electrochemical biosensors have emerged as promising platforms for rapid viral diagnostics, offering high analytical sensitivity, portability, short detection times, and potential compatibility with point-of-care testing. Advances in electrode nanostructuring, biorecognition strategies, signal amplification, and miniaturized instrumentation have enabled remarkably low limits of detection, reaching femtomolar and attomolar concentrations for synthetic viral targets under optimized experimental conditions. However, exceptional analytical performance under controlled conditions does not necessarily translate into clinical diagnostic utility. This review examines the progression of electrochemical biosensors from analytical proof-of-concept toward clinical application, emphasizing the evidence required for successful translation. Following a brief overview of viral targets, recognition strategies, and electrochemical detection approaches, particular attention is given to studies evaluating authentic clinical specimens, including those targeting SARS-CoV-2, dengue virus, human papillomavirus, and hepatitis C virus. Despite encouraging findings, clinical validation remains limited by small sample sizes, incomplete reporting of diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, and insufficient multicentre evaluation, while many platforms have been assessed only using artificial or spiked matrices. Additional challenges include matrix interference, biofouling, reproducibility, sample preparation, manufacturing consistency, stability, workflow integration, and regulatory requirements. Importantly, analytical limits of detection must be interpreted in relation to viral biology, specimen characteristics, clinically relevant thresholds, and intended clinical use. Future research should prioritize reproducible sample-to-answer performance over increasingly extreme analytical sensitivity. Accordingly, this review proposes a staged translational framework encompassing native-matrix analytical validation, adequately powered clinical studies, multicentre reproducibility, manufacturing and usability assessments, and regulatory evaluation. Ultimately, the clinical adoption of electrochemical biosensors will depend on robust evidence demonstrating reliable diagnostic performance in real-world healthcare settings.

title: Cancer screening in solid organ transplant recipients: participation, barriers and facilitators, and strategies to improve routine screening.
abstract: Cancer in solid organ transplant recipients: Over the last few decades, there has been significant short and medium-term improvement in post-transplant graft and patient survival, owing to improved overall patient care. However, in the long term, transplant recipients suffer substantial complications, such as infections, cardiovascular disease (CVD) and cancer. Among these long-term complications, cancer incidence has risen due to enhanced cumulative immunosuppression exposure [1] and broadening transplant eligibility criteria for elderly recipients [2]. These factors increase the overall cancer risk by approximately 2-4 times in transplant recipients compared to the age and gender-matched general population. The cumulative survival after cancer diagnosis at 5- and 10-years post-transplant is only 50% and 20%, respectively [3]. Cancer is also the leading cause of death among solid organ transplant recipients. The cancer occurrence is due to the interplay of several potential mechanisms, such as altered DNA repair, chronic inflammation, impaired innate and adaptive immune function, and loss of immune surveillance secondary to chronic immunosuppression exposure. This leads to an enhanced predisposition for viral infection-mediated and immune-related cancers. The risk for these cancers is time, sex, and site dependent. For example, the cumulative risk for cancer occurrence after 15 years of transplant rises to 10 to 15%. Similarly, at least one skin cancer risk is around 60% in Europe, Australia, and New Zealand [4]. Likewise, the incidence of non-skin cancers is two-fold higher in women than men [5]. The cancer risk also varies with the type of organ affected, such as cervical cancer risk is about 5-10 times, and the risk of developing colorectal and lung cancer is at least two times higher in the SOTRs compared to the general population. However, the risk for breast and prostatic cancers is similar in both populations [6]. Cancer risk is also age-dependent, as older transplant recipients are more likely to get cancer [7, 8]. Compared to the general population, cancers tend to be more aggressive in the transplant population [9], owing to challenging cancer management in the transplant setting due to coexisting comorbidities and the higher treatment-associated risk of rejection and graft loss. Also, a lack of participation in cancer screening has led to the detection of more advanced-stage cancers, which are unamiable to effective management [1]. As a result, overall, the standardised mortality ratio for cancer is 2.7 for transplant recipients [8]. Cancer screening in the solid organ transplant recipients: Cancer screening is defined as earlier detection of cancer in an asymptomatic individual. It has strongly been advocated in the general population as trial-based evidence showed at least a 20% mortality benefit from breast, colorectal and cervical cancer screening. This mortality benefit is due to the availability of potentially curative anti-cancerous therapies for early-stage cancers. Also, the modelled economic evaluation and trial-based evidence reported that breast, colorectal, and cervical cancer screening are cost-effective in the general population [10]. This can be seen from published data, as the incremental cost-effective ratios (ICER) per life year saved for colorectal cancer screening was under 47000 AUD, irrespective of the type of cancer screening modality, among the Australian population [11]. Similarly, the ICER of $28,921 has been reported in the Canadian population with biennially mammographic screening in women aged 50-69 [12]. Also, human papillomavirus DNA testing on the cervical sample has shown to be cost-effective in developing countries, with a reduction in the lifetime risk of cervical cancer by around 25 to 36 per cent and a cost of less than $500 per life-year saved [13]. This has led to the routine adoption of cancer screening in the general population. While there is no trial-based evidence to support routine cancer screening in solid organ transplant recipients, data extrapolated from the general population and observational studies have suggested routine screening may be beneficial and cost-effective. Despite guideline recommendations, uptake for cancer screening remains poor [10, 14, 15]. For example, as seen from the Canadian data, the screening prevalence of colorectal, cervical and breast cancers was 61.6%, 63.4% and 59.9% in the general populations compared to only 22.5%, 30.2% and 8.6%, respectively, in the SOTRs. There may be many reasons that could impact cancer screening participation among SOTRs, which include ongoing health issues, like cardiovascular diseases and infections [16], fears of death after a cancer diagnosis [17], fears of invasiveness of screening tests and radiation exposure, lack of need for screening due to consideration of being healthy, lack of motivation, primary focus on general and graft health maintenance [10, 17], and less awareness about higher cancer risk with a transplant and screening modalities [18]. Additionally, screening is not entirely benign; it can be invasive and detect low-grade cancer that may not cause any symptoms or problems in the future. Overdiagnosis is defined as screen-detected cancer or pre-cancerous condition that would not have progressed clinically during the person's lifetime and would not be harmful if left undetected. It leads to psychological distress and unnecessary investigations like biopsies [10]. Also, transplant recipients experience competing health risks such as chronic comorbidities, high competing death rates, health priorities, the burden of ongoing long-term treatment and certain complications like infections, impacting further their quality of life and survival [19]. Understanding patients' preferences and perspectives on cancer screening is crucial for a shared decision-making process and provides the basis for an individualized approach to cancer screening; both may facilitate cancer screening participation. While discussing cancer screening strategies and options, the importance of providing balanced information about the benefits and potential harms of screening, risks of cancer-related death, and treatment burden have also been stressed to ensure recipient’s ownership of their clinical care and may facilitate improving their cancer screening compliance [19]. Why is it important to do this review: Current observational data highlights potential barriers and facilitators for the low screening uptake in solid organ transplant recipients. Still, a comprehensive review of the reasons, factors, potential interventions, and strategies to improve cancer screening uptake is lacking. In this scoping review, we aim to identify and summarize all the available evidence to gather information about barriers and facilitators for cancer screening participation, performance characteristics of a cancer screening tool, and potential interventional strategies needed to improve cancer screening participation in SOTRs. Knowledge and understanding of the available evidence on the key aspects of cancer screening participation and factors affecting it will enable identifying the core components necessary to propel meaningful changes at the individual, provider, and organizational levels. title: Heme oxygenase and indoleamine regulation by cytokines in cervical cancer cells and natural killer cells cytotoxic activity
abstract: Objective: To determine the effect of the cytokines interleukin (IL-4), IL-10, Interferon gamma (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α) in protein expression of HO-1 and IDO in cervical cancer cell lines and the cytotoxicity of NK cells in co-culture with cervix cancer cells pretreated with HO-1 and IDO inhibitors.Methods: The cervical cancer cell lines HeLa (HPV 18+), SiHa (HPV 16+) and C-33A (HPV -) were treated with 20 ng/mL of IL-4, IL-10, IFN-γ and TNF-α for 3 h, 6 h and 12 h, after that protein expression was assessed by flow cytometry.The cytotoxic activity of NK cells was performed in real time for 4 h.Results: Protein expression of the enzymes were changed at early times, increasing the expression of the enzymes in the 3 cell lines.We observed an increase in cytotoxic activity of NK cells cocultured with HeLa cells pretreated with the HO-1 inhibitor and in SiHa cells pretreated with the IDO inhibitor.Conclusion: The suppressor enzyme IDO is positively regulated by IL-10 in HeLa, SiHa, and NK cytotoxic activity increase in Hela and SiHa cells pretreated with HO-1 and IDO inhibitors respectively, which could be part of tumor escape mechanisms in cervix cancer.

title: Infectious Agents as Drivers of Lung Cancer
abstract: Globally, lung cancer is the most diagnosed cancer and the leading cause of cancer deaths. While tobacco smoke remains the predominant etiological factor for lung cancer, a growing body of evidence implicates chronic infection by specific pathogens as significant co-factors or independent contributors to lung carcinogenesis. This chapter examines the role of infectious agents (Bacteria: Mycobacterium tuberculosis , Chlamydophila pneumoniae , and Helicobacter pylori ; Virus: human immunodeficiency virus, human papillomavirus, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2; and Parasite: Toxoplasma gondii ) in lung cancer development. It reviews molecular mechanisms by which these infections may promote carcinogenesis through chronic inflammation, immune modulation, and direct oncogenic effects. The chapter also addresses co-infections and their interaction with environmental carcinogens, underscoring the importance of studying infectious risks in regions with high burdens of these diseases, including Africa. Finally, the chapter also discusses prospects for prevention strategies (e.g., antimicrobial therapy and vaccination) and the development of novel diagnostic or therapeutic approaches targeting infection-related pathways. Understanding the role of infectious agents provides crucial insights into the multifactorial origins of lung cancer and opens new avenues for risk reduction and intervention.

This chapter examines the role of infectious agents (Bacteria: Mycobacterium tuberculosis , Chlamydophila pneumoniae , and Helicobacter pylori ; Virus: human immunodeficiency virus, human papillomavirus, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2; and Parasite: Toxoplasma gondii ) in lung cancer development. It reviews molecular mechanisms by which these infections may promote carcinogenesis through chronic inflammation, immune modulation, and direct oncogenic effects. The chapter also addresses co-infections and their interaction with environmental carcinogens, underscoring the importance of studying infectious risks in regions with high burdens of these diseases, including Africa. Finally, the chapter also discusses prospects for prevention strategies (e.g., antimicrobial therapy and vaccination) and the development of novel diagnostic or therapeutic approaches targeting infection-related pathways. Understanding the role of infectious agents provides crucial insights into the multifactorial origins of lung cancer and opens new avenues for risk reduction and intervention.

title: EVALUASI TERAPI EKSISI CONDYLOMA ACUMINATA PADA KEHAMILAN: PERSALINAN SEKSIO SESAREA DAN BAYI LAHIR TANPA KELAINAN
abstract: Pendahuluan: Pada kehamilan, Condyloma acuminata (CA) dapat tumbuh dengan cepat dikarenakan perubahan fisiologis pada genitalia eksterna seperti kondisi lembab akibat sekresi cairan vagina yang meningkat, status immunocompromised selama kehamilan, perubahan hormonal dan peningkatan aliran darah ke leher rahim. Ilustrasi Kasus: Seorang wanita berusia 18 tahun, hamil 22-24 minggu, datang ke poli Kulit dan Kelamin Rumah Sakit Umum Daerah Saiful Anwar (RSSA) Malang dengan keluhan benjolan pada kelamin sejak 2 bulan sebelumnya. Awalnya benjolan muncul sebesar biji jagung kemudian membesar dan menimbulkan rasa nyeri dengan Visual analog score (VAS) 4/10. Terminasi kehamilan dengan sectio caesarea (SC) beserta eksisi dengan elektrokauter pada CA dilakukan pada usia 38-39 minggu. Pembahasan: Tatalaksana CA pada kehamilan bertujuan untuk meminimalkan toksisitas pengobatan pada ibu dan janin serta mengurangi gejala. Beberapa studi metaanalisis merekomendasikan terminasi kehamilan dengan SC pada usia kehamilan 38-39 minggu karena peningkatan risiko terjadinya transmisi Human papilloma virus (HPV) melalui darah ibu ke dalam saluran nafas bayi saat persalinan normal. Kesimpulan: Tatalaksana dengan SC meminimalkan terjadinya transmisi vertikal perinatal saat kelahiran. Evaluasi terhadap bayi diperlukan terutama jika terdapat tanda dan gejala yang mengarah ke Juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JRRP) sampai dengan usia 6 tahun.

title: KAT6A promotes malignant phenotypes and attenuates cGAMP-induced type I interferon responses in HPV-positive cervical cancer cells
abstract: Persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) is the principal cause of cervical cancer. However, viral persistence alone does not explain how transformed cells evade cGAS–STING-dependent innate immune surveillance. KAT6A, a lysine acetyltransferase overexpressed in multiple malignancies, remains poorly characterized in cervical cancer. KAT6A expression and its clinical significance in cervical cancer were evaluated through integrated bioinformatics analysis of public GEO datasets and validated in clinical specimens. Stable KAT6A knockdown and overexpression models were established in the HPV-positive cervical cancer cell lines HeLa and SiHa for loss- and gain-of-function studies. The effects of KAT6A on cell proliferation, migration, and apoptosis were examined in vitro, and the association between KAT6A expression and cGAMP-induced type I interferon responses was assessed by qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and ELISA. A xenograft mouse model was used to verify the function of the KAT6A–STING axis in vivo. KAT6A was specifically upregulated in HPV-positive cervical cancer tissues, and its overexpression correlated with suppressed STING pathway activity and poor patient prognosis. Functionally, KAT6A knockdown reduced cervical cancer cell proliferation, migration, and invasion and increased apoptosis, whereas KAT6A overexpression produced the opposite effects. Following cGAMP stimulation, KAT6A knockdown increased IFNβ , CXCL10 , and ISG15 expression and IFNβ secretion, whereas KAT6A overexpression attenuated these responses. These findings indicate that KAT6A modulates cGAMP-induced type I interferon responses but do not establish a direct interaction between KAT6A and STING. This study identifies KAT6A as a regulator of malignant phenotypes and cGAMP-induced type I interferon responses in HPV-positive cervical cancer cells. Further studies are required to determine whether these effects are directly dependent on STING and whether KAT6A influences the tumor immune microenvironment in vivo.

title: Portable gynaecological imaging to enhance naked-eye visual assessment for the management of cervical precancer among women living with HIV in Kenya: An implementation-informed, diagnostic accuracy study protocol
abstract: Background Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries, particularly among women living with HIV (WLHIV). Although visual-based assessment in primary care is feasible and facilitates same-day management, its diagnostic accuracy is dependent on provider experience and skill, resulting in variable performance. Portable gynecological imaging may enhance visual assessment while supporting implementation of cervical cancer prevention in primary care. Methods We will conduct a cross-sectional study among 150 WLHIV co-infected with human papillomavirus and their healthcare providers at Molo Sub-County Hospital in Nakuru County, Kenya. The study will evaluate the agreement between portable gynecological imaging-enhanced visual assessment and conventional colposcopy; estimate diagnostic accuracy using histopathology as the reference standard; determine provider-level acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility, and assess patient-level satisfaction using validated instruments complemented by qualitative interviews and integrated using a sequential, explanatory, mixed-methods approach. Discussion This study will generate preliminary evidence on the diagnostic accuracy and implementation of portable gynecological imaging in primary care. If shown to be accurate, acceptable, appropriate, and feasible, portable gynecological imaging could improve timely identification and management of cervical precancer, and support expansion of high-quality cervical cancer prevention services in similar resource-limited settings.
